StringWithMarkup.String: /LABORATORY ANIMALS: Subchronic or Prechronic Exposure/ Doses of 0, 1, 5, 25 and 100 mg/kg/day /(purity 99.15%)/ were administered in oral gavage during 42 days to SD male rats and from 14 days before mating through day 3 of lactation to female rats. Parental animals receiving 1 or 5 mg/kg/day exhibited no symptoms relating to test substance. NOAEL was established at 5 mg/kg/day dose level. Results applied to both female and male rats. Male rats receiving 25 mg/kg/day showed evidence of hepatocellular swelling and hyaline droplets in the renal convoluted tubular epithelium. In the groups receiving 25 mg/kg/day weights of the /livers and kidneys/ were increased. Hemosiderosis occurred in the groups receiving 25 mg/kg/day. In the dose groups of 100 mg/kg/day there was an overt regenerative process in the renal tubules and increased incidence of atrophic thymus. Increased levels of serum sodium, total protein, total cholestrol; decreased levels of blood urea nitrogen were observed in 100 mg/kg/day dose group. There was also decrease of hemoglobin and hematocrit values. Elevations of urine protein levels were observed in 100 mg/kg/day dose group. There was an evidence of hemolytic anemia in 100 mg/kg/day dose group. In all dosed animals there was no meaningful change of general conditions and no fatal case occurred. The food consumption of 100 mg/kg/day animals decreased on the first day of treatment but showed no significant difference thereafter. There was a decrease in body weight gain.

The test substance was administered via gavage to 8 mated Sprague-Dawley rats at a dose level of 100 mg/kg/day for gestation days 6-12. StringWithMarkup.String: 2,3-Dichloronitrobenzene's former production and use as a chemical intermdiate and production as a byproduct of the nitration of 1,2-dichlorobenzene may result in its release to the environment through various waste streams. If released to air, an estimated vapor pressure of 5.0X10-3 mm Hg at 25 °C indicates 2,3-dichloronitrobenzene will exist solely as a vapor in the atmosphere. Vapor-phase 2,3-dichloronitrobenzene will be degraded in the atmosphere by reaction with photochemically-produced hydroxyl radicals; the half-life for this reaction in air is estimated to be 321 days. 2,3-Dichloronitrobenzene absorbs light at wavelengths of 310 nm and therefore may be susceptible to direct photolysis by sunlight. If released to soil, 2,3-dichloronitrobenzene is expected to have low mobility based upon an estimated Koc of 1,100. Volatilization from moist soil surfaces is expected to be an important fate process based upon an estimated Henry's Law constant of 1.2X10-5 atm-cu m/mole. Biodegradation half-lives in excess of 4 weeks using activated sludge suggest that biodegradation is not an important environmental fate process. If released into water, 2,3-dichloronitrobenzene is expected to adsorb to suspended solids and sediment based upon the estimated Koc. Volatilization from water surfaces is expected to be an important fate process based upon this compound's estimated Henry's Law constant. Estimated volatilization half-lives for a model river and model lake are 42 hours and 17 days, respectively. A BCF range of 82 to 151 suggests bioconcentration in aquatic organisms is moderate to high. Hydrolysis is not expected to be an important environmental fate process since this compound lacks functional groups that hydrolyze under environmental conditions. Occupational exposure to 2,3-dichloronitrobenzene may occur  through inhalation and dermal contact with this compound at workplaces where 1,2-dichlorobenzene is produced. (SRC)

Section.Description: Sorption to soils and sediments is an important factor on the transport and fate of organic contaminants in the environment.  The soil/water adsorption coefficient, also known as solid-water distribution coefficient (Kd), measures the amount of chemical substance adsorbed onto soil per amount of water.  Since adsorption occurs predominantly by partition into the soil organic matter, it is more useful to normalize the Kd value to the organic carbon content of a soil and express the distribution coefficient in Koc (organic carbon normalized distribution coefficient).  The greater the Kd (or Koc) value, the less likely a chemical will leach or contribute to runoff.  A very high value means it is strongly adsorbed onto soil and organic matter and does not move throughout the soil.
